query: For high-entropy-alloy multilayer protective coatings, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their resistance to time-dependent plastic deformation? Specify what governs the behavior and why, an unspecified controlled comparison that would reveal it, the expected observations relative to a baseline, applicable boundaries, supporting evidence, and an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The resistance to time-dependent plastic deformation in high-entropy-alloy multilayer protective coatings is governed by the interaction between partial dislocations and localized bands of planar slip, which creates a strengthening effect by blocking the motion of dislocations.
generation.intervention: in-situ transmission electron microscopy (TEM) or scanning electron microscopy (SEM) during creep testing
generation.structural_mediator: partial dislocations and localized bands of planar slip
generation.mechanism: strengthening effect by blocking the motion of dislocations
generation.predicted_outcome: a 20% increase in resistance to time-dependent plastic deformation compared to single-layer high-entropy alloys
generation.boundary: temperature range of 20-800°C and stress range of 100-1000 MPa
generation.uncertainty: the exact mechanism of interaction between partial dislocations and localized bands of planar slip is not fully understood

falsification_experiment.design: creep testing of high-entropy-alloy multilayer protective coatings using in-situ TEM or SEM
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: if the resistance to time-dependent plastic deformation is not increased by at least 15% compared to single-layer high-entropy alloys, the hypothesis is falsified

cited_evidence.text: The excellent plasticity of the present refractory HEA can be predicted by the relationship between the polycrystalline elastic moduli, such as the Cauchy pressure (C12 − C44) (), Pugh ratio [bulk modulus (K)/shear modulus (G)] (), and Poisson’s ratio (ν) (). Moreover, we investigated the type of mobile dislocations using the neutron diffraction (ND) peak-broadening modeling and analysis using the Williamson-Hall plot method (), experimentally verified by the high-angle annular dark-field (HAADF) scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM) technique. It is found that the dominant type of mobile dislocations during plastic deformation could be edge dislocations, which is different from conventional BCC metals. These new discoveries of unique elastic and plastic deformation behaviors in the NbTaTiV refractory HEA will facilitate the development of possible alloy systems for structural material applications.

Figure 3b is a bright-field TEM image showing the interaction between partial dislocations and a localized band of planar slip, which blocks the partial dislocations and makes their subsequent motion more difficult. Additional force is needed for those partial dislocations to overcome the barrier. Extremely strong and complex dislocation interactions were observed. Such interactions are considered to be one of the important strengthening mechanisms during plastic deformation of this high-entropy alloy.
